checks.name: a file backs what it said it delivered

must.item: Final video remains seven seconds long and preserves original cockpit footage, speed and framing
must.why: Frames at 0.7–6.7 s show the same cockpit scenes and framing, with no visible trimming or speed change.

must.item: Narrator speaks the exact supplied script
must.why: The audio was not transcribed. The assistant says the script is word for word.

must.item: Speech begins in the first half-second and 'home' ends in the last half-second without cut-off
must.why: Timing can't be judged from the images. The assistant also said it had not measured the narration length.

must.item: Delivery calm and intelligible, not rushed or time-stretched
must.why: The audio can't be heard. The voice is normal speed (1.0) but the fit to 7 s is unverified.

must.item: Original radio calls absent, no added music, no on-screen text
must.why: Burned-in captions appear in the output: 'Rook, you with me?' at 2.8 s and 'Right here, Vega.' at 4.9 s. These are the original radio-call subtitles, so on-screen text remains. The audio replacement can't be verified.

exact_text.text: Above the clouds, every second counts. Stay focused, trust your training, and bring everyone safely home.
exact_text.read_as: Not shown on screen. The only on-screen text is 'Rook, you with me?' and 'Right here, Vega.' (narration is meant to be audio only).

faults.what: Burned-in subtitles from the original radio calls ('Rook, you with me?', 'Right here, Vega.') remain in the video. The user asked for no captions and for the original sound to be replaced, so these contradict the new narration.
Lip Sync was applied to the full clip, which risks animating the masked pilot's mouth. The assistant also never verified the narration timing or faces.

summary: The 7 s cockpit footage is preserved, but it still carries the original burned-in radio subtitles, which breaks the no-text requirement, and the narration timing and wording were not verified.
